content.paragraph: In trying to find the volume of a solid we face the same type of problem as in finding areas. We have an intuitive idea of what volume means, but we must make this idea precise by using calculus to give an exact definition of volume.

subsection.title: Definition of Volume
subsection.paragraph: We start with a simple type of solid called a cylinder (or, more precisely, a right cylinder). As illustrated in Figure 1(a), a cylinder is bounded by a plane region $$B_{1}$$ , called the base, and a congruent region $$B_{2}$$ in a parallel plane. The cylinder consists of all points on line segments that are perpendicular to the base and join $$B_{1}$$ to $$B_{2}$$ . If the area of the base is $$A$$ and the height of the cylinder (the distance from $$B_{1}$$ to $$B_{2}$$ ) is $$h$$ , then the volume $$V$$ of the cylinder is defined as

In particular, if the base is a circle with radius $$r$$ , then the cylinder is a circular cylinder with volume $$V = \pi r^{2}h$$ [see Figure 1(b)], and if the base is a rectangle with length $$l$$ and width $$w$$ , then the cylinder is a rectangular box (also called a rectangular parallelepiped) with volume $$V = lwh$$ [see Figure 1(c)].

figure.alt_text: A three-dimensional rendering of a solid. The top and bottom surfaces of the solid resemble parabolic areas and are labeled B_2 and B_1, respectively. The back side of the solid is a rectangle with a height of h. The front surface of the solid is a curved rectangular surface that connects the other three sides. A three-dimensional rendering of a cylinder of radius r and height h. A three-dimensional rendering of a rectangular box has a length l, width w, and height h.

subsection.paragraph: For a solid $$S$$ that isn’t a cylinder we first “cut” $$S$$ into pieces and approximate each piece by a cylinder. We estimate the volume of $$S$$ by adding the volumes of the cylinders. We arrive at the exact volume of $$S$$ through a limiting process in which the number of pieces becomes large.

We start by intersecting $$S$$ with a plane and obtaining a plane region that is called a cross-section of $$S$$ . Let $$A(x)$$ be the area of the cross-section of $$S$$ in a plane $$P_{x}$$ perpendicular to the $$x$$-axis and passing through the point $$x$$ , where $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . (See Figure 2. Think of slicing $$S$$ with a knife through $$x$$ and computing the area of this slice.) The cross-sectional area $$A(x)$$ will vary as $$x$$ increases from $$a$$ to $$b$$ .

figure.alt_text: A three-dimensional rendering of a solid, labeled S, is graphed on the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. The x axis has 3 tick marks, labeled a, x, and b, from left to right. The solid resembles a loaf of bread, with its length along the positive x axis and an inward fold along its length and its tip cut off. It begins directly above the tick mark a and ends directly over the tick mark b. The plane cuts the solid and its cross-sectional area, labeled A(x), is shaded. The ends of the solid which are directly above the marks a and b are labeled A(a) and A(b), respectively.

subsection.paragraph: Let’s divide $$S$$ into $$n$$ “slabs” of equal width $$\Delta x$$ by using the planes $$P_{x_{1}},{P_{x_{2}},\ldots}$$ to slice the solid. (Think of slicing a loaf of bread.) If we choose sample points $$x_{i}^{*}$$ in $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ , we can approximate the $$i$$ th slab $$S_{i}$$ (the part of $$S$$ that lies between the planes $$P_{x_{i - 1}}$$ and $$P_{xi}$$ ) by a cylinder with base area $$A(x_{i}^{\ast})$$ and “height” $$\Delta x$$ . (See Figure 3.)

subsection.paragraph: The volume of this cylinder is $$A(x_{i}^{\ast})\Delta x$$ , so an approximation to our intuitive conception of the volume of the $$i$$ th slab $$S_{i}$$ is
Adding the volumes of these slabs, we get an approximation to the total volume (that is, what we think of intuitively as the volume):

This approximation appears to become better and better as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . (Think of the slices as becoming thinner and thinner.) Therefore we define the volume as the limit of these sums as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . But we recognize the limit of Riemann sums as a definite integral and so we have the following definition.

note.paragraph: Let $$S$$ be a solid that lies between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ . If the cross-sectional area of $$S$$ in the plane $$P_{x}$$ , through $$x$$ and perpendicular to the $$x$$-axis, is $$A(x)$$ , where $$A$$ is a continuous function, then the volume of $$S$$ is

subsection.paragraph: When we use the volume formula $$V = \int_{a}^{b}A(x)dx$$ , it is important to remember that $$A(x)$$ is the area of a moving cross-section obtained by slicing through $$x$$ perpendicular to the $$x$$-axis.

Notice that, for a cylinder, the cross-sectional area is constant: $$A(x) = A$$ for all $$x$$ . So our definition of volume gives $$V = {\int_{a}^{b}}Adx = A(b - a)$$ ; this agrees with the formula $$V = Ah$$ .

subsection.title: Volumes of Solids of Revolution
subsection.paragraph: If we revolve a region about a line, we obtain a solid of revolution. In the following examples we see that for such a solid, cross-sections perpendicular to the axis of rotation are circular.

problem.paragraph: Did we get a reasonable answer in Example 2? As a check on our work, let’s replace the given region by a square with base $$\lbrack 0,1\rbrack$$ and height $$1$$ . If we rotate this square, we get a cylinder with radius $$1$$ , height $$1$$ , and volume $$\pi \cdot 1^{2} \cdot 1 = \pi$$ . We computed that the given solid has half this volume. That seems about right.

problem.paragraph: The region $$\mathcal{R}$$ enclosed by the curves $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^{2}$$ is rotated about the $$x$$-axis. Find the volume of the resulting solid.
